new_statements.quote: 2.3 Tonal features Emai is a terraced-level tone language showing high, low, and downstepped high. For some word classes, inherent tone values distinguish words that in all [...] Various combinations of tone occur within lexical items. An initial high tone can be followed by a low tone, a high tone, or a down stepped high, the latter being one step lower [...] orthographic practice, high tone is represented by an acute accent, low tone by a grave accent, and down stepped high by an acute accent immediately [...]

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (in_catalog false, existing_statements empty). Snippet-level only: a tonal description with no stress statement; consistent with the on-file Emai tone papers (Schaefer & Egbokhare 1994 ERIC ED375640, PLSA 2021-2026) that treat Emai as tonal. A full reading of sketch 2.3/3 still requires the lending copy or the paid PDF.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The sketch describes Emai as a terraced-level tone language with high, low and downstepped high tones, lexical and grammatical tone, tone marked orthographically by acute/grave accents; the searchable text of the whole book returns zero hits for 'stress', 'stressed', 'unstressed', 'word stress', stress* and 'prominence', and the two 'accent' hits are orthographic diacritics, so the work makes no word-stress statement (as far as the scanned search layer shows).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (no stress vocabulary anywhere in the searchable text)
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary and its sketch describe the Emai lect proper (Emai clan, Afuze area, Edo State) of the Glottolog languoid Emai-Iuleha-Ora; sketch section 1 mentions Ora and Iuleha only as co-members of Elugbe's (1973) dialect cluster; Uokha is never named (0 FTS hits).

sources.citation: Schaefer, Ronald P. & Francis O. Egbokhare. 2022. Secondary concepts and internal dynamics of Emai serial verb constructions. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 65. doi:10.5842/65-1-976
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Only orthographic tone conventions (acute = high, grave = low, acute+downstep) and 'non-contour, level tones (high or low) on polysyllabic verbs'; no stress.

Studies in African Linguistics 42(1). doi:10.32473/sal.v42i1.107275; Schaefer & Egbokhare 2021 Metatony (PLSA 6, doi:10.3765/plsa.v6i1.5000); Schaefer & Egbokhare 2023 Preverbs (PLSA 8, doi:10.3765/plsa.v8i1.5507); Schaefer 1986 Reference point marking in Emai (ERIC ED285405); Schaefer & Egbokhare 2002 Emai sentence complements (ERIC ED468597)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Syntax/semantics papers; each only restates the tone-marking convention (high = acute, low = grave, downstep = acute + apostrophe); a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence finds nothing relevant in any of them.

sources.citation: Schaefer, Ronald P. & Francis O. Egbokhare. 1994. Emai verbal and preverbal tone: preliminaries. Paper, 25th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, New Brunswick, March 1994. ERIC ED375640, 16 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Tone only: 'two significant level tones low and high', rising/falling from juxtaposition; verbs, auxiliaries and monosyllabic preverbs are lexically toneless and get surface tone by rule. Zero mentions of stress/accent/prominence (only 'accent' in a reference title).

sources.citation: WALS Online, language 'Emai' (wals code ora, glottocode emai1241), sources Donwa-Ifode 1990 and Schaefer & Egbokhare 2007.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Emai is coded for 11 WALS features (10A, 81A-95A, 116A) but NOT for the stress chapters 14A-17A; no secondary stress datum exists.

sources.citation: Donwa-Ifode, Shirley O. 1990. Transitional phonologies and their implication for orthographies: the case of Ora. Journal of West African Languages 20(2): 3-18.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Segmental sketch of Ora ('My data is based on Emai', p. 3): 7 oral + 7 nasal vowel phonemes, consonant inventory, vowel sequences, nasalisation, orthography. Tone appears only in the discussion of the floating high-tone genitival linker (pp. 15-16). Nothing on stress, accent or prominence.

sources.citation: Schaefer, Ronald P. & Francis O. Egbokhare. 2026. Mood: tonal and segmental realization in Edoid. Proceedings of the Linguistic Society of America 11(1). doi:10.3765/plsa.v11i1.6059
